summary.summary: Kirklees' debt keeps climbing: external borrowing rose £42.8m to £816.8m in 2025/26 (against a £987.2m capital financing requirement), funded by £90m of new PWLB loans at 4.59%-4.72% and £32.5m of medium-term loans from other councils, while treasury investments halved to £30.2m. £96.5m of loans fall due within 12 months against that £30.2m of cash, and the council says it will keep borrowing short-to-medium term while long rates stay high. The year had genuine positives: a £5.5m treasury budget underspend and a restructuring that prepaid £40m of Barclays loans for £29.5m — a £10.5m discount worth £2.1m in NPV savings. It still holds £30.8m of LOBO loans (none called in-year) and a £10m CCLA property fund position carrying £1.3m of unrealised losses behind the statutory override, now expected to run to April 2029.

signals.headline: External borrowing up £42.8m to £816.8m at 31 March 2026; £90m new PWLB plus £32.5m of local-authority loans taken in-year
signals.why: The CFR is still rising with the capital programme (£987.2m), so Kirklees is a committed repeat borrower.

signals.headline: £96.5m of loans mature within 12 months of 31 March 2026 (up from £75.2m a year earlier), by a deliberate short/medium-term borrowing strategy while long rates are high
signals.why: A growing short-dated stack must be rolled at whatever rates prevail after the sharp market moves of March 2026.

signals.headline: Treasury investments halved to £30.2m at 31 March 2026 (from £58.6m), against £816.8m of debt and £96.5m maturing within a year
signals.why: Year-end cash covers less than a third of the debt due in the next 12 months, leaving little buffer for shocks.

findings.paper_title: Q1 2026-27 Council Plan and Performance Update Report V1
findings.headline: Local unemployment has risen 54% year-on-year to 5.1%, above regional average of 4%
findings.detail: Unemployment reached 5.1% in Q3 2025/26, up from 4.2% in Q2 2025/26 and 3.3% in Q3 2024/25. This 54% year-on-year increase significantly exceeds the Yorkshire and Humber regional average of 4% and indicates local labour market deterioration.
findings.matters: Rising local unemployment cascades into multiple council financial pressures: reduced business rates, increased welfare demand, housing arrears (already rising 3.59%), homelessness pressure, and potential council tax collection risk. It is a leading indicator of worsening fiscal stress.
findings.quote: Unemployment Rate: Performance 5.1% (11,300 / 221,569) (Q3 2025/26) - Worse than Q2 2025/26 (by 0.9 pp) - Worse than Q3 2024/25 (by 1.8 pp)

findings.paper_title: Q1 2026-27 Council Plan and Performance Update Report V1
findings.headline: Children in Need caseload surged 26% year-on-year: 570 additional cases in Q1 2026/27
findings.detail: Children in Need reached 2,735 in Q1 2026/27, up 570 (26%) from Q1 2025/26 and 347 (14.6%) from Q4 2025/26. This statutory safeguarding metric shows strong upward trend with no explanation provided for drivers of demand growth.
findings.matters: Children in Need is a leading indicator for children's social care cost growth and escalation to child protection. A 26% year-on-year increase in a service already flagged as having structural cost pressures will translate into higher assessment, plan, and support service costs.
findings.figures: 2,735 children in need (up 570 year-on-year, 26% growth; up 347 quarterly, 14.6% growth)
findings.quote: Number of Children in Need: 2,735 (Q1 2026/27) - Increase on Q4 2025/26 (by 347 children) - Increase on Q1 2025/26 (by 570 children)

findings.paper_title: Q1 2026-27 Council Plan and Performance Update Report V1
findings.headline: Housing Register demand growing sharply: 1,554 more applicants year-on-year (7.5% growth)
findings.detail: Housing Register applicants reached 22,209 in Q1 2026/27, up 1,554 from Q1 2025/26 and up 320 from Q4 2025/26. This rapid growth signals increased housing stress and will drive future demand for temporary accommodation, affordable housing delivery, and housing management resources.
findings.matters: Rapid housing register growth indicates growing housing insecurity in the population. This directly drives temporary accommodation spending, capital commitments for affordable housing, and creates potential future homelessness pressure. It correlates with rising unemployment and tenant arrears.
findings.figures: 22,209 applicants Q1 2026/27 (up 1,554 from Q1 2025/26; 7.5% annual growth)
findings.quote: Number of applicants on Housing Register: 22,209 (Q1 2026/27) - Increase on Q4 2025/26 (by 320 applications) - Increase on Q1 2025/26 (by 1,554 applications)

findings.paper_title: Q1 2026-27 Council Plan and Performance Update Report V1
findings.headline: Tenant arrears rising: 3.59% of rent due, up from 3.38% a year ago
findings.detail: Housing rent arrears reached 3.59% (£3.79m of £105.6m due) in Q1 2026/27, up from 3.38% in Q1 2025/26. This deterioration is occurring despite reported positive trends in direct debit uptake and proactive arrears management. The rise correlates with unemployment increasing to 5.1% (up from 3.3% year-on-year).
findings.matters: Rising tenant arrears are a leading indicator of household financial stress. Combined with 54% unemployment increase in the same period, this signals genuine economic stress in the tenant population that will worsen further if economic conditions deteriorate.

findings.paper_title: Q1 2026-27 Council Plan and Performance Update Report V1
findings.headline: Home to school transport costs rising: 4% annual demand growth alongside deteriorating contract market
findings.detail: Home to school transport pupil numbers grew 4% (63 pupils) comparing Q1 2025/26 to Q1 2026/27, reflecting ongoing SEND population growth. The service faces 'challenging market conditions for private contracts' which means 'the service is continuing to see increased costs' despite ongoing efficiency improvements and use of in-house provision.
findings.matters: This is a statutory, demand-driven service with rigid entitlements. Combining 4% annual pupil growth with deteriorating contract market creates structural cost inflation that cannot be controlled through efficiency. A lender would see this as uncontrollable recurring spending.
findings.figures: 4% increase (63 pupils) Q1 2025/26 to Q1 2026/27; ongoing upward trend in SEND population
findings.quote: Comparing Quarter 1 of 2025/6 to Quarter 1 of 2026/7 shows an increase overall of 63 pupils or a 4% increase in numbers accessing the service... challenging market conditions for private contracts, means the service is continuing to see increased costs.
